cards.54.who: HM, PM, Data. Source: network effects; Section 9.5. Scored on: understanding product statistics at a high level.
cards.54.why: It names the network interference problem correctly, gives three options by feature type, takes an ethical view (don't hold back protection), and is humble in the right place.
cards.54.five: Spot the leak, give three options by feature type, and take an ethical stance on safety features.
cards.54.evidence: ✅ Section 9.5. 🟨 hands-on A/B testing experience: be honest about how much you have.
cards.54.image: Lab: **two test tubes** joined by a **leaking pipe** (leak), and next to them **a shield that is never taken off** (ethics).
cards.54.locus: Room G, the test tube rack.
cards.54.must: (1) the leak; (2) three types; (3) ethics for safety features; (4) working with a data scientist.
cards.54.traps: Not seeing the network effect problem. Suggesting you turn off scam warnings for the control group.
cards.55.who: CEO, HM. Scored on: vision, a link to the business, realism, and humility because you don't know the inside yet.
cards.55.understand: The trap: presenting a vision too confidently about a product you haven't seen. A senior person gives **one clear picture** + **three pillars** + **"I'd test this against what you know"**.
cards.55.why: One vision line in the user's own words (the CEO can remember it), three pillars that each have a concrete picture, "Local, at global standard" ties straight to the G-local principle, and a humble close.
cards.55.five: One vision line in the user's words, three pillars, and "outside-in, I'd test it". Speak slowly.
cards.55.evidence: ✅ Sections 2, 9.8. 🟦 the vision is not tested; this is an outside-in view.
cards.55.hook: **"My people, nothing bad gets through."** Calm · Protected · Local at global standard. "C-P-L: Cà Phê Lê Duẩn" (coffee on Lê Duẩn).
cards.55.image: Balcony: you look down at **a quiet café** (calm) on Lê Duẩn, with **a guard at the door** (protected), serving **phin coffee in an international porcelain cup** (local at global standard).
cards.55.must: (1) the one-line sentence; (2) three pillars; (3) design system + team; (4) outside-in, will test it.
cards.55.drill: Speak slowly. 90 seconds. Stand up straight when you practise.
cards.55.traps: A "super app" vision. Being too sure. Not tied to Vietnamese users.
cards.56.who: HM, CEO, HRBP. Scored on: a realistic plan, learning before doing, a quick win.
cards.56.why: Three keywords that are easy to remember, each stage has concrete actions and an output, there is a quick win, and the last line "the thing I won't do" signals someone who has watched new hires fail.
cards.56.five: Bring the 30-60-90 plan on one A4 page; have a concrete quick win; "won't redesign everything".
cards.56.evidence: ✅ Hearti Lab (built a team from scratch). ✅ AI adoption lead (started by listening).
cards.56.image: Balcony: **three plant pots**, small, medium and large (30, 60, 90). The first pot has **an ear**, the middle one has **a flower in bloom**, and the big one has **a milestone post**.
cards.56.locus: Room H, the three plant pots.
cards.56.must: (1) three stages; (2) an output for each stage; (3) one concrete quick win; (4) don't redesign everything.
cards.56.drill: Write the plan on one A4 page and bring it with you.
cards.56.traps: Jumping into action in week one. No quick win.
cards.57.who: CEO, HM, PM. Scored on: realistic product strategy thinking.
cards.57.understand: The honest answer: **almost nobody "switches"** away from Zalo; people **add** an app when they have a reason. A senior person says this plainly and proposes a **wedge**: one specific situation where the product wins.
cards.57.why: The opening is frank and true (CEOs like people who don't flatter). There's a short look at competitors. There are three concrete "wedges" to test, tied to how people in Vietnam behave. It shows that chat grows by groups. It ends with design's role.
cards.57.five: "Nobody switches, they add", three wedges, and when asked, pick one and explain the growth loop.
cards.57.evidence: ✅ Sections 2, 9.8. ✅ Zalo has about 75-78 million MAU. 🟦 the wedges are hypotheses; you don't know their strategy.
cards.57.image: Balcony: looking down at the street, **a wooden wedge** is jammed into **a giant Zalo-blue door**. Coming through the gap: a family, a shop owner, a doctor.
cards.57.must: (1) nobody switches; (2) nobody owns trust; (3) three wedges; (4) groups, not individuals.
cards.57.drill: Pick the wedge you believe in most and prepare a 2-minute explanation in case they ask you to go deeper.
cards.57.traps: "We'll be better at everything". "Super app". Criticising Zalo.
cards.58.who: HM, HRBP. Source: reviews mention changes of direction and managers who disagree. Scored on: handling ambiguity, taking initiative.
cards.58.why: There's a concrete action ("write it down, ask to be corrected"), it turns ambiguity into choices, it protects the team by keeping "lasting" work apart from "bets", and it has evidence from lab and startup settings.
cards.58.five: "Wrong draft beats blank page" + keep lasting work apart from bets + one piece of lab/startup evidence.
cards.58.evidence: ✅ LSEG Innovation Labs, Hearti Lab. 🟨 decision log: only mention it if you really did it.
cards.58.image: Balcony: the wind blows **a draft sheet of paper** away, and you **pin it down with three clips** (three options).
cards.58.must: (1) write it down so people can correct it; (2) three options; (3) keep lasting work apart from bets; (4) evidence.
cards.58.traps: Complaining. Waiting to be told what to do.
cards.59.who: CEO, HM. Scored on: business thinking, numbers.
cards.59.why: The opening line says clearly how design creates value. Two examples with numbers, one about revenue (lead-to-sale) and one about productivity. The last line links to Qualgo's business model.
cards.59.five: Two examples with numbers labelled correctly (relative/absolute), linked to Qualgo's model.
cards.59.evidence: ✅ Merchant 70%, +20%. 🟨 **confirm that +20% is relative and that 70% is onboarding time for existing customers (T6).** ✅ Fulfilment.
cards.59.image: Balcony: **a cash register** pops out the numbers **70** and **+20**, and next to it **a whole family** is stepping into the lift.
cards.59.must: (1) definition; (2) two examples with numbers; (3) link to Qualgo.
cards.59.traps: Taking all the credit. Not knowing if a number is relative or absolute.
cards.60.who: TA, HRBP, HM. Scored on: self-awareness, honesty, actively working on it.
cards.60.understand: Pick a weakness that is **real and relevant, but not fatal**, and that has **evidence you're fixing it**. The review in Section 6 points to B5: **talking too long and in too much detail**. This is a good choice: it's real, the interviewer may have already seen it, and you have evidence that you're fixing it (Toastmasters). Don't use "haven't done chat" here, because you already said it in Q5.
cards.60.why: It's real and self-aware, has light humour ("you may have noticed"), three concrete actions, evidence (Toastmasters), and a closing invitation that makes you feel closer to the listener. The line "It's not fixed" is the imperfect detail that makes people believe you.
cards.60.five: Under 45 seconds, "better, not fixed", and you really do keep your answers short for the whole interview (proof through behaviour).
cards.60.evidence: ✅ Toastmasters VP Education 2023-24, President 2024 to now. ✅ B5 in Section 6.
cards.60.image: Director's office: a **long paper scroll** rolls out of your mouth all the way to the door, and **Toastmasters scissors** cut it short.
cards.60.must: (1) a real weakness; (2) why it happens; (3) three actions; (4) "better, not fixed".
cards.60.drill: This answer must be under 45 seconds, or you've just proven the weakness.
cards.60.traps: "Perfectionist". "I work too hard". A fatal weakness (for example "I don't like conflict" for a Lead role).
cards.61.who: HRBP, CEO. Source: B12 (short time in roles), Singapore salaries are higher than in Vietnam. Scored on: commitment, real motivation.
cards.61.why: It reuses the fact that "they reached out first" as proof of commitment, turns the gap into a reason to stay (a smart move), and the personal reason of "going home" is very convincing to a Vietnamese interviewer.
cards.61.five: Three reasons, and "moving home" is confirmed as a real plan.
cards.61.evidence: ✅ Qualgo reached out 2-3 times. ✅ about 15 years in Singapore. 🟨 **"move home" must match your real plan** (a role in Saigon? remote work? moving the family?). Confirm the work location before you say it.
cards.61.image: Director's office: **a suitcase** lies open and the clothes are already **put away in the wardrobe** (staying for a long time).
cards.61.must: (1) said no before; (2) still learning, so will stay; (3) going home.
cards.61.drill: Say it in a warm voice, not a defensive one.
cards.61.traps: "I'm not overqualified" (denial). Promising too much ("I'll stay ten years").
cards.62.who: TA (R1, very early), HRBP (at the end). Scored on: being realistic, not breaking the deal.
cards.62.understand: This is the only question where the best answer depends on **information you don't have yet**. Principles from negotiation (Harvard Program on Negotiation; Fisher & Ury, *Getting to Yes*): **know your BATNA** (staying at NAB is a strong BATNA), **let them give a number first if you can**, talk about the **total package**, and **use your strong card, "they reached out to you", once and gently**. Details in Section 13.4. 🟦 **Before R1, set your minimum (walk-away) number and your target number**: convert your current total income in Singapore, and work out living costs and tax in Vietnam.
cards.62.why: You have a strong BATNA (you're doing well at NAB, and they came looking for you), so you're in a position to ask for the budget range first. Saying "total package" opens up other levers besides base salary. Giving full notice is a sign of professionalism (they'll get the same treatment one day).
cards.62.five: No pause before the number (under 1.5 seconds); ask for the budget range first in R1; talk about the total package and the exact notice period.
cards.62.evidence: 🟨 **notice period at NAB.** 🟦 **target and minimum numbers (do this on Day 10).** 🟨 work arrangement (Vietnam / remote / Singapore).
cards.62.image: Director's office: **an offer envelope** on the table, and you **gently push it back towards them** so they open it first.
cards.62.must: (1) ask for the budget range; (2) total package; (3) full notice.
cards.62.drill: Say your number out loud 10 times until you stop pausing. A pause = an invitation to push you down.
cards.62.follow_ups.0.a: **"I'd rather focus on the value of this role than my current pay, which is in a different market and structure. I'm happy to share my expectations."** (in some places this question is restricted; in Vietnam it's common, so keep it friendly)
cards.62.traps: Giving a number before you know the scope. Giving a number that's too low because you want the job. Pausing. Threatening them with another offer that doesn't exist.
cards.63.who: HRBP, HM. Source: your CV shows freelance work, Toastmasters, ADPList. Scored on: conflict of interest, focus.
cards.63.understand: You do freelance work for a stablecoin wallet (fintech, which may overlap with Qualgo's "secure transactions"). They need to know two things: is there a conflict of interest, and will it take your focus away? Answer **openly**, with **a clear plan**.
cards.63.why: Being open before they ask (the "Act with transparency" value), a concrete plan for the freelance work, and community activities framed as a benefit.
cards.63.five: Open before they ask, and a freelance plan you've checked you can actually do; your declaration status with NAB is confirmed.
cards.63.evidence: ✅ freelance, Toastmasters, ADPList. 🟨 **have you declared the freelance work to NAB yet (T13)?** 🟨 **can you finish or hand over the freelance work (what did you promise the client?)?** Don't say "wrap up" if you can't do it.
cards.63.image: Director's office: **a drawer pulled wide open** (openness), and inside is a wallet (freelance) with **a label saying "close before day 1"**.
cards.63.traps: Hiding the freelance work. Naming the client without permission.
cards.64.who: HM, HRBP. Source: reviews (changes, long tests, slow feedback); you come from a big bank. Scored on: adapting, not needing structure.
cards.64.why: It turns the assumption around (you're not a pure "bank person"), gives two pieces of startup evidence, and turns banking experience into an advantage ("just enough structure").
cards.64.five: Turn the "bank person" assumption around with two pieces of startup evidence and "just enough structure".
cards.64.evidence: ✅ Hearti Lab (3 products, 15 projects). ✅ stablecoin wallet. ✅ LSEG Innovation Labs.
cards.64.image: Director's office: **a lacquer painting** hangs crooked on the wall, and you **nudge it just enough** to make it straight, without putting a new frame on it.
cards.64.must: (1) you've worked in places with little structure; (2) two pieces of evidence; (3) "just enough structure".
cards.64.traps: "I love chaos" (nobody believes it). Speaking badly about bank processes.
cards.65.who: CEO, HM. Source: reviews show interviewers from Shopee and Binance; Qualgo will see candidates from VNG/Zalo, MoMo, Shopee. Scored on: confidence, a clear difference, respect for rivals.
cards.65.understand: This question compares you directly with candidates who are stronger than you in consumer chat. Don't put them down. Name **three things you have that they find hard to match**, admit **what they have**, and suggest **a way to combine both**.
cards.65.why: The opening admits the rival's strength (real confidence), three differences with evidence tied to Qualgo's strategy (trust, AI, working across disciplines), and the close suggests a team, which shows you're thinking like a Lead.
cards.65.five: Admit the rival's strength in the first sentence in a calm voice, three differences with evidence, and end with "both".
cards.65.evidence: ✅ all of it. ✅ Qualgo is hiring for agentic AI and GenAI.
cards.65.image: Director's office: **two chairs** face the desk; the other chair has **a Zalo uniform shirt** hanging on it; you **pull the two chairs closer together**.
cards.65.drill: Say the opening line in a calm voice, with a smile.
cards.65.traps: Putting down other candidates. Not admitting the gap. Talking too long.
cards.66.who: Every round. Scored on: curiosity, how well you prepared, judgement.
cards.66.understand: This is **your turn to ask**, but it's still part of the interview. Good questions show you're assessing them too. Pick **two questions** that fit the interviewer (full list in Section 13.1).
cards.66.answer:
| Person | Question |
|---|---|
| TA Linh | *"What does the full process look like from here, and what's the timeline?"* · *"What made the team reach out to me specifically?"* |
| HM Khoa | *"What would make you say, in a year, that hiring me was the right call?"* · *"What's the biggest disagreement on the team about the product right now?"* |
| PM Mai | *"How do product and design decide what to build next quarter?"* |
| Mobile Eng Tuấn | *"What's the most painful part of design handover today?"* |
| Senior Designer Vy | *"What would you want from a design lead that you're not getting now?"* |
| Security/AI Hằng | *"Where does AI run today: on the device, in the cloud, or both? And who decides?"* |
| CEO | *"What does success look like in two years, and what's the biggest risk to getting there?"* · *"How do the Vietnam team and international partners decide together?"* |
| HRBP Ngân | *"How has the role been shaped over the past year? I noticed it's been open a while."* |
cards.66.why: Each question is written for one person, which shows you did your research. The question "What would you want from a design lead…" for Vy turns someone who might be wary of you into an ally. The question about why the role has been open so long, asked politely, helps you find out the truth.
cards.66.five: Two questions written for the person in front of you, you take notes on their answers, and you ask one follow-up based on what they just said.
cards.66.hook: **"Two questions, the right person."** HM: "right call in a year". Vy: "what you're not getting". CEO: "biggest risk".
cards.66.image: Director's office: **a suggestion box** on the desk, and you **pull out two letters**, each with one person's name on it.
cards.66.must: (1) at least two questions; (2) they fit the person asking; (3) take notes on the answers.
cards.66.drill: Learn the questions for the HM, Vy and the CEO by heart.
cards.66.traps: "No, I think you covered everything." Asking the HM about salary or leave. Asking about things that are on the website.
cards.67.who: Every round, especially HM and CEO. Scored on: the last impression (the recency effect).
cards.67.understand: Research on memory (the serial position effect, Murdock 1962) shows that listeners remember best what comes first and what comes last. Your closing is what they take into the debrief. Prepare **a 45-second close**: sum up three reasons, admit one gap and how you'll fill it, and one sentence that shows you want this.
cards.67.why: It repeats the two reasons to say "yes" from Section 5 (trust + AI), admits the gap one last time (the listener has already thought of it, so you answer it first), and ends with a direct, emotional line that brings back the fact that they reached out first.
cards.67.five: Word for word, 45 seconds, and look the listener in the eye on the last line.
cards.67.image: You walk out of the director's office, **turn back**, and put **a blue ✓✓** (read) on the desk.
cards.67.locus: Room I, the exit door. The end of the floor 18 tour.
cards.67.must: (1) three reasons; (2) gap + how you fill it; (3) "I've finished. I'd really like to do this with you."
cards.67.drill: Learn it word for word. This is the only answer in the book you should memorise exactly.
cards.67.traps: "No, I think that's all." Going through your whole CV again. Sounding desperate ("I really need this").
cards.68.who: HM, PM, CEO, Security/AI. Source: the brand JD says "AI-powered secure communication and transactions". Scored on: understanding money risk in a social setting, and using your banking and wallet experience.
cards.68.understand: This is the question where you have the biggest edge over every candidate from a chat app: you've designed send-money flows (stablecoin wallet), bank onboarding (NAB Merchant) and maker-checker controls. The real issue is this: *chat speeds up trust, and scammers use exactly that speed.* The design has to keep chat feeling natural while still adding one "slow moment" in the right place.
cards.68.why: The opening names the right paradox (chat builds trust faster than the user can check it), it has a before/during/after structure, it uses **two real pieces of your own evidence** (wallet, maker-checker), and it has one sharp idea that's easy to remember ("send in 10 minutes").
cards.68.five: You need all three: a *single* slow moment (rather than many layers of friction), one piece of evidence from the wallet or the bank, and fraud as the guardrail, rather than conversion alone.
cards.68.evidence: ✅ Stablecoin wallet (send/receive, confirmation). ✅ NAB Merchant onboarding, maker-checker. 🟦 The "cooling-off" and "notify a family member" ideas are your proposals, not features you've shipped.
cards.68.image: Rooftop railing: **a red lì xì envelope** tied to **a 10-minute hourglass**.
cards.68.must: (1) the trust-speed paradox; (2) the confirmation screen: amount, verified recipient, whether it can be reversed; (3) wallet/bank evidence; (4) fraud guardrail.
cards.68.drill: Sketch the confirmation screen in 3 minutes. Add it to P1.
cards.68.traps: Talking about blockchain or stablecoins (off topic). Adding friction at every step. Promising "we'll refund scam victims".
cards.69.who: PM, CEO, Vy. Source: "mass audience" in the brand JD; older people are the main victims of scams. Scored on: empathy with a method, without talking down to people.
cards.69.answer:
**"I design for them as experts in their own lives who are new to this interface, not as people who need protecting from themselves."**

Four practices. Plain Vietnamese, not translated English: "Tin nhắn từ người lạ", not "Message request". One primary action per screen when something is risky. Generous type and touch targets, tested with font scaling at maximum on a mid-range Android. And recognition over recall: show who someone is, with a photo and how you know them, rather than expecting people to remember.

Then I test with them directly. In preparing for this interview I tested a scam-warning concept with five people, two of them over fifty-five, and the biggest learning was [🟦 your real finding].

The quiet benefit: designs that work for a sixty-year-old in Cần Thơ work better for everyone in a hurry.
cards.69.why: The opening respects users (the assessor will notice how different it is from a talking-down tone), four concrete practices, evidence from a real test, and a closing line about designing for everyone.
cards.69.five: One real finding from P3, told as a quote from a user.
cards.69.evidence: 🟦 P3 (test with 5 people). ✅ Accessibility experience (52 colours at LSEG).
cards.69.image: Railing: grandma's **reading glasses** tied next to **a button as big as your hand**.
cards.69.must: (1) respect; (2) four practices; (3) a finding from a real test.
cards.69.drill: 60 seconds, with a quote from P3.
cards.69.traps: "Elderly users struggle with technology." Suggesting a separate interface straight away.
cards.70.who: HM, Vy, CEO (very likely in R2 or R3 if the product already has a beta). Scored on: a sharp eye, respect, setting priorities, and how you talk to the person who made it.
cards.70.understand: The person in the room may be the one who designed it. The goal is to show that **you see the most important thing and talk about it like a colleague**, rather than to find as many problems as you can.
cards.70.why: Thinking out loud shows your method, specific praise comes first, there are only two problems and they're in priority order, and the line "what I don't know" protects your relationship with the person who may have designed it.
cards.70.five: The number 1 issue you pick must be about trust or first use, and you ask *"Was that a deliberate choice?"* before suggesting anything.
cards.70.evidence: 🟦 Practise with P2 (teardown) and by critiquing 3 apps you don't know, 3 minutes each. ✅ Q20 (same structure).
cards.70.image: Railing: **a hand mirror** with **two sticky notes** stuck on it.
cards.70.must: (1) think out loud; (2) one specific good point; (3) two problems in priority order; (4) a question about constraints.
cards.70.drill: Every evening for the last 3 days: critique an app you don't know in 3 minutes, and record yourself.
cards.70.traps: Listing 10 problems. Criticising the visuals before you understand the flow. Proposing a full redesign.
cards.71.who: HM, Eng, CEO. Source: the "Own" culture; a security product, where incidents are serious. Scored on: staying calm, ownership, learning in a structured way.
cards.71.understand: 🟨 **It must be a real story.** Good options: Fulfilment after go-live, Merchant onboarding after launch, or a release at Hearti Lab or LSEG. The frame below uses a **Contain · Explain · Change** structure (like the blameless postmortem that is common in engineering).
cards.71.why: The three-step structure is the language of engineers and leaders; "blameless" shows you understand a healthy incident culture; admitting design's part shows ownership.
cards.71.five: You say *design's share of the fault* in one sentence, you blame no one, and you have a habit you still keep.
cards.71.evidence: 🟨 **Choose a real story before Day 11 (Story Forge in the game).**
cards.71.image: Railing: a red **fire extinguisher** with a "postmortem" label on it.
cards.71.must: (1) the first action; (2) design's part; (3) the change and the habit.
cards.71.follow_ups.0.a: 🟨 your real answer; the principle: **"Early, plainly, with what we know and when we'll know more."**
cards.71.traps: A story with no real consequences. Blaming engineering or a vendor.
